q-104533.name: Question 1
q-104533.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{tan}⁡y$ that lies between $y=0$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
q-104533.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=0$ to ${y}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡y)={sec}^{2}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}y\sqrt{1+{({sec}^{2}⁡y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}y\sqrt{1+{sec}^{4}⁡y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

b

EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since we're given a curve in the form x=f(y), we have

ds=1+(dxdy)2dy. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy.

We are told that the limits of integration are from y1=0 to y2=π4.

Computing the derivative, we get

dxdy=ddy(tan⁡y)=sec2⁡y.

Finally, we obtain

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy=2π∫0π/4y1+(sec2⁡y)2dy=2π∫0π/4y1+sec4⁡ydy.

q-109145.name: Question 2
q-109145.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that lies between $y=0$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
q-109145.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=0$ to ${y}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}y\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve x=sin⁡y that lies between y=0 and y=π3. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
2π∫0π/3y1+cos2⁡ydy
b
2π∫0π/3sin⁡y1+cos2⁡ydy
c
2π∫0π/3cos⁡y1+sin2⁡ydy
d
2π∫0π/3y1+sec2⁡ydy
e
2π∫0π/3y1+sin2⁡ydy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since we're given a curve in the form x=f(y), we have

ds=1+(dxdy)2dy. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy.

We are told that the limits of integration are from y1=0 to y2=π3.

Computing the derivative, we get dxdy=ddy(sin⁡y)=cos⁡y.

Finally, we obtain S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy=2π∫0π/3y1+cos2⁡ydy.

Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts (see figure above). What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
q-109186.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =\pm n\pi ,\,n\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

S=∫2πyds.

ds=1+(dxdy)2dy. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy.

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the y-axis by solving the following equation:

sin⁡y=0y=±nπ,n∈Z

Hence, we need to integrate from y=0 to y=π.

Computing the derivative, we get

Finally, we obtain

q-109257.name: Question 4
q-109257.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ that lies between the lines $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
q-109257.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=-1$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}2\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi x\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\pi [1-(-1)] \\  & =8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve y=4−x2 that lies between the lines x=−1 and x=1. Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis.

a
 8π
b
 4π
c
 π2
d
 π3
e
 12π

Correct

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since we're given a curve in the form y=f(x), we have

ds=1+(dydx)2dx. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫x1x2y1+(dydx)2dx.

We are told that the limits of integration are from x1=−1 to x2=1.

Computing the derivative, we get

dydx=ddx(4−x2)=−x4−x2⇒(dydx)2=x24−x2.

Therefore,

S=2π∫x1x2y1+(dydx)2dx=2π∫−114−x21+x24−x2dx=2π∫−114−x244−x2dx=2π∫−112dx=4πx|−11=4π[1−(−1)]=8π.

q-109269.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=3.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
q-109269.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})=\frac{1-x}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{1-2x+{x}^{2}}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})\sqrt{1+\frac{1-2x+{x}^{2}}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})\sqrt{\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{\sqrt{x}(3-x)}{3}(\frac{x+1}{2\sqrt{x}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3-x)(x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3+2x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {[3x+{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
